Until then, what's it worth?

But you will need to know what the group can offer in the way of water, housing, food stores, health care, tools, seasonal labor, transportation, access to markets, schooling, etc. Do you have outside debts to pay? How long will your cash reserves last, if the community uses them? What critical skills will you need? Being great at the emotional stuff won’t stop you from being dead in the water if the one person who knows where everything is and how it works gets too exhausted to keep going.

Please Choose the Values Before Falling in Love With the View

Have you noticed people often choose their community in the same way they would choose a vacation rental? “Wow! Look at this beautiful land! And a pond, with the sunset in it!! Who needs a beach?! And the people seem really nice, let’s get in here!” Fast forward two years. “Wait, there’s a vaccination policy?? And you need paperwork for it?!?!”

Bring your values with you when you go to visit a community. Make a list of what you really believe about children, money, property ownership, romance, medicine, food, spiritual practice, technology, privacy, dealing with conflict, leaving the community, etc. It’s a long list, I know. Some of them will just get a question mark, if you’re not sure yet.

Sexuality and gender belong on there too. Would LGBTQ+ people be able to live openly in your community, date, be in relationships, and stay fully protected by the community? Should children be taught to question their sexual identities from a young age, and what happens if one of the community’s children comes out as gay or transgender? Until you answer these, your community’s values on freedom and on raising children aren’t complete. Yep. Both of them.

Are you willing to experiment? That’s a real value too. Put it on your list, because the people you live next to might think the experiment ended in 1978, and everything that came out of it is doctrine now.

Then don’t just listen to what the group says. Look at how they really operate. A recent conflict is a good place to start: how did they handle it? There’s also who can block decisions, and what happened to the last person who left. (And who owns the land!) Does that match your values? It’s uncomfortable to talk about these things, I know, but the view isn’t going anywhere.

Resources, Land, and Exit Terms

Who will have title to the land? Very important! Whoever has it will have enormous power over the rest of the community. If the deed is in the name of the founder, then he or she is really a landlord with a philosophy. If three out of twelve members own everything, then whether or not your literature says everyone is equal, there are two classes of members.

What kind of legal entity (cooperative, trust, association, company, whatever fits your jurisdiction) will hold the land? This needs to be decided before it's bought. Then you'll need to decide who has what voting rights, who has what access and use rights to common resources, how you will account for people's contributions (if at all), how inheritance works, what about outside debt, how improvements get handled, and what happens when someone wants to leave the community. Lots of decisions to make!

And how will you handle the visibility of what the community has? A money-free community still has scarce things and bottlenecks, sorry. It will be important for people to know what's owned or held in common, what you've set aside, what obligations you have to outsiders, who has authority to hand out the major resources, where conflicts of interest are, etc. It won't do to have the transfer of major resources (land, equipment, stores, outside cash, etc.) dependent on one person's memory or permission.

Good people leave for good reasons -- dying parent, love, work, health, exhaustion, change of mind, etc. You don't want them to lose everything they've put in. That's coercive -- they HAVE to stay if they can't afford to go. Whether or not you use money, you'll need to have a way of providing people with resources when they leave (cash, if you use it, but also tools, transportation, temporary housing, stored up goods, the right to keep using something, or whatever). Otherwise their "right" to leave is only on paper -- it only works when the community happens to have spare money. Write up the exit terms while leaving is still only theoretical -- like a pre-nup when you're planning the wedding. Not romantic, but protective. Much easier than doing it once anybody's furious.

Honestly? For the nuts and bolts of all this (members, resources, land, agreements, etc.), I'd go to Diana Leafe Christian's Creating a Life Together (on the reading list at the end).

From Visitor to Member—Slowly

When The Farm grew fast, a lot of the people who came were in need, and there weren’t many filters that worked. Being open to everybody felt so spiritual! The practical burden piled up anyway. A membership process is there to protect both the people who are already there and the newcomers.

First, correspond with them. Did they read the materials? (Not everyone does.) Do they get the basic idea of why this community is here? Are they at least starting to do the relevant practices? It’s a lot cheaper to find out through a thoughtful exchange than after six months of misunderstanding, right?

The short visit: If they come for a week or two and just participate in normal life, well, most people can be charming for two weeks. Not exactly a high bar. 😅 So that's about all you'll find out.

The long visit: If you're not around long enough to actually experience inconvenience and conflict with the person in question, then you're not going to learn very much about them. Watch how they react when tired, corrected, attracted, disappointed, bored, etc. (Hopefully not all at once!) Even a professional faker may be able to pull off an act for months.

Write down your answers: How long is a provisional membership, and what are a provisional member's rights and responsibilities? How is it reviewed, and how does someone leave it? Who decides on full membership? (Hint: not the person who recruited them! 😜) And what rights does a full member have to the land, the shared resources and a voice in the group, and what do they owe over the long term? (Those go in your founding agreements.)

At each stage, always judge people based on their conduct. No matter how good it sounds when they talk about their spirituality or their therapy, don’t go by that. What do they actually do? It’s too easy to go by vibes. It’s also easy to think someone’s safe just because they’re going along with everyone else. Six months with someone will give you more data, but there’s still no “good person” detector.

If someone will have a role in your group that has serious consequences, involving kids, shared resources, medicine, vehicles or private records, you want to know how they handle that specific thing. I wouldn’t hand someone the van keys just because they’re great with kids. You can find out by checking whether you’ve seen them do this thing before, and asking for references if appropriate. Give people access to these things in stages and ensure there’s always some way to appeal decisions about these roles to a separate authority if needed.

Do stuff together prior to making them provisional members. (Sorry, hanging out doesn't count. I know, it's the fun part.) Can you actually make a decision as a group? Can you actually work together to get something done (an ordinary work or shared-resource task will do)? Can you even process a small conflict afterwards? Do a trial run like that before anybody sells their house to move in. It can show you whether your way of coordinating works.

Then there are the people who aren't fully "in" the commune politically. Visitors, volunteers, workers, renters and interns at the commune (yes, even interns) are entitled to some rights when decisions really affect their pay or access to common resources. Why wouldn't they be? All of them should have clear terms, and the chance to be heard and to have such decisions reviewed. The same is true for decisions really affecting their schedule, safety, housing, records or discipline. Equality that stops at the membership line can end up recreating a servant class that moves from commune to commune.

When Somebody Has to Go

A safe community can’t promise to keep everyone. There may be times when someone has to go. Yeah, it’s tough. It’s also true. If someone is a serious or generalized danger to others, or keeps violating essential boundaries, or for whatever reason just makes everyday life together impossible for everyone else, it can be the right call to eject them. If restorative work can help in a reasonable amount of time, all the better. But it’s not the community’s job to be a treatment program for someone who’s endangering everyone else.

This power to remove people is so easily abused, though. So work out the process before it's about anyone in particular. What counts as cause for immediate protective action? Who decides to put temporary restrictions on someone? Who will make sure all the evidence is preserved? Who will recuse themselves? How will the person be able to reply to the concerns, and have the decision reviewed or appealed without putting others in danger? What protections will there be for the person’s interests (housing, records, family contact, access to common resources, outside funds if any) during the separation? When is it time to bring in outside help? (More on that next.)

Note that "outside" doesn't have to mean the nation-state. My research initially leaned too far that way. The basic need here is for a competent level of authority that is not reviewing its own conduct. That could mean another community, a federation of communities, professionals, autonomous regional institutions, courts, regulatory agencies, emergency services, etc. The key is that it's not the same people. An important correction that came from the Zapatistas: that authority can be an autonomous regional institution, without it turning into the state. And no, autonomy still doesn't mean anyone gets to decide that individual people don't have certain non-waivable rights, or that outside jurisdiction just goes away.

Also decide on a mediator or ombudsperson in advance. Why bother? People often won't trust someone they haven't already met, who comes in during a crisis as a "neutral stranger." A mediator doesn't obviate the need for evidence, safeguarding, rulings, etc. Mediation is an attempt to restore good relations between people. When people can't or won't consent to being in community any more, they still need a final separation.

What This Looks Like From Sénégal

The “African Renaissance Monument” in Dakar, Sénégal, which stands at 160 feet tall and took 4 years to build.

I live in Sénégal, where "intentional community" often sounds like a strange Western phrase. People here are like, "Don't human beings already do that?"

Sénégal is unlike anywhere else I've lived. Five times a day the prayers pour out into the streets. I find them so soothing. And Sufism doesn't stay inside designated "spiritual" places here. It's in the music, in the pictures everywhere, in the murals, in the names, in the conversations.

And the humor! People are outside laughing for hours at a time. This is the most joking culture I've ever been in, and I keep wondering if I'll ever understand the really complicated jokes in Wolof. Basic conversation is one thing. But knowing why twelve people are suddenly crying with laughter? That's graduate school.

In the villages and families I've spent time around, so much is taken care of by the extended family and the local memory, alongside the formal systems. Whether it's land, childcare, housing, food, obligations, etc, etc. Who needs a workshop called "Rebuilding Intergenerational Belonging" when some aunt has already given three people a task?

Even in Dakar, I found this graffiti on a wall: "Tolerance! Openness! Union! Happiness! Love!" And elsewhere there are murals of Sufi leaders. Spiritual graffiti still surprises me. Where I grew up, a city wall was either selling you a product or showing off somebody's inability to draw a penis.

Graffiti in Dakar, Sénégal: Tolerance! Openness! Union! Happiness! Love!

All is not well in paradise

But does this mean I think Sénégal is some magical place that's kept its communal paradise? No, not quite. The warmth has hard limits here. One noteworthy example is the plight of LGBTQ+ people here, who cross them automatically.

Sénégal passed a law in March 2026 (Law No. 2026-08) that increased the penalty for "consensual same-sex intimacy" to 5 to 10 years in prison, and it also made public advocacy for homosexuality a crime. Homosexuals were already facing arrests, family rejection, harassment, assault and mob violence, so ironically, some say they're actually safer once they're arrested, because then at least the mob can't get at them. And also ironically, LGBTQ+ people are using this prejudice in their favor to get refugee status and live in rich countries. Anyway, I'm not going to praise communal belonging and ignore the people who have to hide who they are to survive it, or leave.

So which is it? Well, in a way, it's both. It's possible for a society to be spiritually alive, generous, funny and super communal, while still becoming cruel to those who break its social categories. Being in community isn't automatically liberating. It all depends on who is allowed to belong without pretending.

One other shadow side of the otherwise forgiving social culture here is that people may go to great lengths to avoid confrontation. Who stole the sheep? We all know, but nobody wants to cause a stink by bringing it up.

Where I live, neighbors steal our moringa pods every morning. Every morning! They could plant a moringa tree in their own yard. Apparently maintaining this relationship with ours is more entertaining. 😂

Everybody here has sheep (even me), and they are super cute. It can feel like you're living in another world, with the music, the animals, the joking, the praying, and just being around people all the time.

Of course, the old communal ways here are changing. Young people move to the city, get a job, get a phone, eat imported food, become part of the wider world, etc. (some of the men even make the dangerous journey by sea to Europe). So what about the families? The ones that used to share almost everything are now more reliant on cash and individual opportunities.

Lessons from the Black Tax

Then there's the so-called "Black Tax," a strange legacy of the old communal system: if you've got any money at all, you're expected to share it with your parents, your siblings, your cousins, to pay school fees, medical bills, funerals, etc. I understand the instinct. In the ancestral way of doing things nobody made it alone, and the people who fed and raised you had a real claim on whatever prosperity came through you later. So why not share in return? That's how the whole organism survived (it wasn't charity).

But these days it can be soul destroying. People have a lot less of the communal life that held the obligation up (the shared land, work, childcare, food and daily belonging), but they still carry it. So if one of them makes it into the cash economy, it's really hard to build any independence or long-term stability, because they may be expected to carry everybody. How can they get ahead, when all these people are dependent on them? And the relatives stay dependent too, since the payments don't give them a real alternative. It's the ancestral ethic playing out inside an individualistic cash economy. It can keep people alive, but it eats away at both sides too.

This is also the thorny boundary issue of living without money inside a money-based society. Life inside the commune can go without cash, but you'll still need money for taxes, hospital bills, visas, school fees, family obligations, buying in tools etc. That doesn't mean going back to individual wages inside the commune, but it does mean someone has to handle it. Who's that going to be? And the commune has to work out how much shared cash it keeps for these things, and how to stop access to outside money from creating a new status hierarchy.

Another aspect of outside work, even before there's a common purse, is that it's not just money you're bringing into the commune. You're also bringing in a different schedule, a different status system, a different social world, different loyalties, and often different consumption habits etc. etc. And you can't exactly leave all that at the door, can you? In the first stage, where people working outside should contribute an agreed share, it's really important that they can't use the money to buy their way out of everyday communal work, or to buy a greater say in the political system. It's also important that the group notices when outside jobs start draining the people and skills it needs to build the communal livelihoods. Otherwise the commune will stay a dormitory for the money economy instead of moving toward a common purse.

Some Zapatista communities used to try to stop their young people from leaving, which is a version of the same outside-work problem. Now they talk it through with them instead: it's OK to go and work elsewhere, as long as the migrants keep certain defined obligations to the community. That doesn't make the pull between leaving and belonging go away, but at least now it's something they can name and negotiate. I understand the motivation to negotiate like that, but I think it's not a full solution either.

Westerners often start out isolated and try to rebuild a tribe. A lot of Africans start out with a communal life they inherited, and watch parts of it fall apart. Kind of the opposite problem. And urban Africans who get interested in intentional community might come to it feeling alienated from both the city and the tradition they left.

So this is a global issue, far from some Western lifestyle niche. There's still knowledge in the living villages that no book can give you. But if you visit, remember they're people, not museums. Would you like people coming to your house to stare at you and your family? So be respectful, contribute something, learn the language, and don't expect anyone to hand you a spiritual service package.

Oh, and a practical note: getting my residency in Sénégal was pretty cheap and straightforward. French and Wolof matter a lot more than English. And the country's famous ideal of Teranga (hospitality) is real in my life. I'm staying in a friend's family's house, and they won't let me pay rent! Can you believe it? Of course that generosity lives right alongside watchfulness, social conservatism, bureaucracy and all the usual complications of a real country.

Practice Comes Before Property

Most people try and do community in the wrong order. "First let's get land!" "Then let's write down a vision document!" "And whoever's putting in the money can own the place!" And the emotional side of things? That doesn't get done until "later on, when everyone has more time".

It would be better to get together to practice first, and process a real conflict, and get clear on your values, and test membership, and decide ownership and exit, and then, after all that, think about land. Less cinematic, I know. (It would make for a pretty bad movie.)

Same with money: do it in stages. Don't try and fly right to the economic destination in one go. Wait until the group can reliably provide for everyone, and fairly decide who gets what from the common, before it goes to a common purse. And work on reducing (or eliminating) outside money based on what the group has shown it can do, rather than by declaring "money is impure!" (That sounds kind of weird when somebody else is paying the tax bill.)

If You Can’t Move

I realize that for most people reading this there are a lot of reasons why they can't just head off and go build community on some land. Jobs, kids, pets, debt, a mortgage, a sick parent, or several of these arranged in a circle... That's fine! The most important pl/ork doesn't need land anyway.

Too bad you can’t move…

People sometimes buy forty acres and then bring all their unprocessed stuff with them to a more scenic location. It's a more beautiful view for sure, but now you have the conflict PLUS goats.

So your inner pl/ork can start now, right where you live. Peer counseling takes two people and a private place to sit and talk. And reparenting, somatic work, jealousy work, conflict repair, etc etc? None of it has to wait until somebody has a deed in hand.

A group that practices together weekly for two years may never own land. So what? It can still make a difference when people are going through a divorce, an illness or grief. Parenting too, and plain old loneliness.

Here's an idea if you're remote, or stuck where you are: build the part of community you actually can. Have a weekly meal with two households. Set up a counseling exchange with one friend, in person or by video. Share tools or childcare. Transport or food prep work too. Or a sauna. And if you're hippie enough, add acro-yoga, dance improv, a mothers' circle or a cuddle puddle.

Trust me on this one. If three households keep showing up for each other like this for six months, you'll learn more than you would from another year of daydreaming about the ideal village.

What to Do This Month

So what do you actually do this month? Start doing some inner pl/ork, with the free reparenting guide and Hearthwork manual or with another serious practice you already trust. And practice before you have an audience.

Find two or three other people and meet regularly. Call it a practice group, not a commune. Practice listening and switching roles. Get through at least one disagreement too, and keep your commitments. You can talk about a shared future later.

Where do you find these people? Try an unprogrammed Quaker meeting, a restorative-practice group, an open-hearted congregation, a mature recovery group, a meditation group, or find some people who have gone on long retreats and come back kinder, rather than more impressed with themselves.

Go visit some real communities. Really, go! Twin Oaks is one. East Wind is another, and so is Acorn, and there are plenty of other intentional communities. Lots of ecovillages are open to visitors too. Check their current visitor requirements first.

By visiting some communities, you'll get a better idea of how much togetherness you enjoy and what kind of privacy you need, and what kind of labor system irritates you. And whether communal showers feel liberating, or make you start looking at studio apartments! No manifesto is going to tell you any of that!

Look before you leap. It will really save you some time & money.

I'm not trying to sell you a retreat or get you to fill out an application or anything. The manuals I mentioned are free. I've just noticed that wherever people are taking real care of each other and playing, feeling useful and having room to become more honest, community tends to gather.

Decades after the Bruderhof shaped my father, I'm publishing the film he made, and writing this.

Maybe some of you will build something useful from this. Maybe that community will teach someone else, who'll build another. Passing it on doesn't need one institution or one founder. And there doesn't have to be one official version of it, either.

If you build something real, maybe we'll hear about each other. And if you teach other people to build, hearing about it matters less.

They may disagree about politics, food, God, sex, or whether shoes are oppressive, but they agree that something about the current arrangement is starving them.

Communes Are Hot Again 🔥

Suddenly the longing behind my father’s movie is everywhere again, and in 2023 the U.S. Surgeon General even put out an advisory about it. Or about the loneliness under it, at least. The advisory said roughly half of American adults experience loneliness, and it treated social connection as a public-health issue.

Whether you want to call that loneliness an official “epidemic” or not, it’s obvious that a lot of people can’t tolerate modern life in isolation anymore (it's literally classified as torture by the UN's Geneva Convention). They may disagree about politics, food, God, sex, or whether shoes are oppressive, but they agree that something about the current arrangement is starving them.

Check out the Google Trends for “ecovillage” and “intentional community”. After years of decline, interest climbed sharply in the mid-2020s.

I have no proof that the rise of AI caused this turn, but it’s hard to ignore the coincidence in timing. AI became serious around this time, and it started changing people’s jobs and relationships, and how they see the future. Suddenly, forming a village sounded like a good backup plan, not just a hippie utopian whim.

It’s poppin’ on Instagram too! 🔥 Chantress Seba—my favorite light-language love influencer—posted an application for people interested in starting a commune. I applied, although I don’t think she’s coming to Africa, where I'm at. When I saw the post, many thousands of people appeared to be interested. Imagine opening your inbox after casually inviting a million followers to co-found a village.

Later, when another influencer with a big following floated the commune idea, the comment section started to become a recruitment board. It was chaotic, but sincere, and it was revealing. There were people in the comments finding prospective members the way you’d usually find a used sofa.

The Freeloader Problem

Some of the commenters weren’t trying to join. The oldest objection, that maybe most people don’t want to take on the responsibility that anarchism requires and communal property becomes “owned by everyone, cared for by nobody,” showed up almost right away.

The commune comments became a miniature political-philosophy seminar, as Instagram comments sometimes do.

I'd say the comment above is more true of the big socialism experiments than small communes, but I still take it seriously, because some people really would rather let somebody else take responsibility. When everybody owns everything, it can get to where nobody knows who's supposed to do what, and the same three people end up doing all the maintenance while everybody else talks about freedom. And then unofficial leaders start gaining power. Partly that's because everyone keeps handing it to them.

Communal ownership entails folks taking on visible and named stewardship duties. It requires knowing what to do if someone is leeching off the group and how to deal with it. It requires developing healthier forms of relationships. No, taking away the idea of a boss does not make everyone less passive, selfish, thieving, nor suddenly unlearning learned helplessness.

People want to go back to the old way of living, but they have no idea why earlier communes failed or what to do when someone wants to own land, the group runs out of money, a baby is born or jealousy rears its head. They just know they are tired and alone and want to change it.

I am not currently recruiting anyone or founding a community, which makes it easier for me to write an article like this, since I’m not trying to get you onto my land. I do plan to buy land, and people may naturally end up living around me. All of the warnings in this article apply to me, too.

Whether you want to call that loneliness an official “epidemic” or not, it’s obvious that a lot of people can’t tolerate modern life in isolation anymore (it's literally classified as torture by the UN's Geneva Convention). They may disagree about politics, food, God, sex, or whether shoes are oppressive, but they agree that something about the current arrangement is starving them.

What's starving them is anomie. We evolved to live in small groups where everybody knows everybody. In a large society the shared norms and close ties that held those groups together fall apart, and that's how large societies end up run by psychopaths. (Yes, I'm always going on about this.)

Check out the Google Trends for “ecovillage” and “intentional community”. After years of decline, interest climbed sharply in the mid-2020s.

I have no proof that the rise of AI caused this turn, but it’s hard to ignore the coincidence in timing. AI became serious around this time, and it started changing people’s jobs and relationships, and how they see the future. Suddenly, forming a village sounded like a good backup plan, not just a hippie utopian whim.

It’s poppin’ on Instagram too! 🔥 Chantress Seba—my favorite light-language love influencer—posted an application for people interested in starting a commune. I applied, although I don’t think she’s coming to Africa, where I'm at. When I saw the post, many thousands of people appeared to be interested. Imagine opening your inbox after casually inviting a million followers to co-found a village.

Later, when another influencer with a big following floated the commune idea, the comment section started to become a recruitment board. It was chaotic, but sincere, and it was revealing. There were people in the comments finding prospective members the way you’d usually find a used sofa.

The Freeloader Problem

Some of the commenters weren’t trying to join. The oldest objection, that maybe most people don’t want to take on the responsibility that anarchism requires and communal property becomes “owned by everyone, cared for by nobody,” showed up almost right away.

The commune comments became a miniature political-philosophy seminar, as Instagram comments sometimes do.

I'd say the comment above is more true of the big socialism experiments than small communes, but I still take it seriously, because some people really would rather let somebody else take responsibility. When everybody owns everything, it can get to where nobody knows who's supposed to do what, and the same three people end up doing all the maintenance while everybody else talks about freedom. And then unofficial leaders start gaining power. Partly that's because everyone keeps handing it to them.

Communal ownership entails folks taking on visible and named stewardship duties. It requires knowing what to do if someone is leeching off the group and how to deal with it. It requires developing healthier forms of relationships. No, taking away the idea of a boss does not make everyone less passive, selfish, thieving, nor suddenly unlearning learned helplessness.

People want to go back to the old way of living, but they have no idea why earlier communes failed or what to do when someone wants to own land, the group runs out of money, a baby is born or jealousy rears its head. They just know they are tired and alone and want to change it.

I am not currently recruiting anyone or founding a community, which makes it easier for me to write an article like this, since I’m not trying to get you onto my land. I do plan to buy land, and people may naturally end up living around me. All of the warnings in this article apply to me, too.
